lines.text: What if you got $1,000 every time you said no?
A man in a yellow vest holds out a flyer. Free pizza slice with any large order?
No, thanks. Your phone buzzes. Deposit received, $1,000.
You stop in the middle of the sidewalk, you look at the screen. Then at the man, he shrugs.
Your loss, you look at him. Say that again, free pizza slice?
No, buzz, another $1,000. The man backs away slowly, like you might be contagious.
Yeah, something is seriously wrong here, but let me explain.
Right now, you're 16. You work weekends at a hardware store.
You have a best friend named Theo, a mom who works two jobs, and a little sister named Zoe, who still believes you can hear her through the wall.
Your savings account holds exactly $212, and you have never in your entire life been good at saying no,
which is why the morning that started all this was so strange. At breakfast, Zoe asked if you would trade her your last waffle.
You said no, your phone buzzed. You said, wait, what?
Zoe said, is that a yes? No, buzz.
Zoe looked at you like you had grown a second head, and then she ate the waffle anyway.
Three buzzes before eight in the morning. So you do what any reasonable person would do.
You test it. Here is how it works. Every time you say no, you get $1,000.
But there are rules. The no has to be out loud. The no has to be real.
Saying it to an empty room does nothing. You tried that for 10 minutes, and the only thing you earned was a very worried look from your cat.
Someone has to genuinely want a yes. They have to be hoping even a little.
A robocall doesn't count because no human is hoping for anything.
The universe, it turns out, only pays you to disappoint a real person.
And then there is the second rule which you find out by accident. At lunch, Theo asks you to hand him the salt.
You say sure, buzz, withdrawal, $1,000, gone.
Every no pays you. Every yes costs you the same.
So what if you could earn $1,000 every time you said no?
Let's find out. The first week is the best week of your life. At school, a teacher asks for a volunteer to erase the board.
Nobody moves. You raise your hand and say, I'll do it, withdrawal, $1,000 to erase a whiteboard.
Never again. So you learn the game. Say no to the lunch lady's extra fries, plus 1,000.
Say no to the guy selling magazine subscriptions, plus 1,000.
Say no to the petition about the school fountain, plus one.
By Friday, you have $41,000 and you haven't done anything except be annoying.
Let's do the math. If someone asks you something every minute and you say no every time, that is $60,000 an hour.
A typical full-time worker in America earns about $60,000 in a whole year.
You are doing it before your lunch break is over. And that is when you get ambitious.
There is only one problem. You need people to ask you for things.
So you go looking for the most persistent people on earth. Telemarketers, real humans, not robocalls.
Americans get billions of robocalls a month and you sit on hold to find the ones where an actual person picks up.
You call a car warranty company, a man named Gary Answers.
Hello, I'm calling about your car's extended warranty. No, buzz, sir, it's a very good deal.
No, buzz, sir, please, no, buzz, sir, I have a family.
No, buzz, Gary has a family, you still get paid. You are not proud of this.
You hire a guy to stand next to you at the mall and ask, every 10 seconds, do you want a cookie?
He has paid $20 an hour. You are paid $180,000 an hour.
After two hours, he asks if you want to switch. No, buzz.
By the end of the month, you have $22 million. You pay off mom's loan.
She reads the letter from the bank three times and she sits down on the kitchen floor and cries.
You buy Theo's family a new roof and Theo's dad pretends the whole time that he isn't crying too.
Remember that by the way, his dad, he comes back.
Quick reality check, around a third of Americans say they couldn't cover a surprise $1,000 expense.
A single no from you pays that bill. And yes, the IRS has already sent you a very polite email.
Money from saying no is still income. For a while, it feels like the greatest loophole in history.
Then the quiet starts. Here's what you didn't notice when you say no for a living.
The people around you stop asking. It starts with small things.
Theo invites you to the lake. You say no, buzz.
He tries again on Saturday. No, buzz. He tries again on Sunday.
No, buzz. On Monday, he doesn't ask.
Mom asks if you'll come to dinner on Sunday, like every Sunday for the last 16 years.
No, buzz. Her face does something you've never seen.
She says okay, not angry, just okay. And then she doesn't ask the next week either.
Psychologist Vanessa Bohn spent years studying what happens when people ask for favors.
She found that the person asking almost always underestimates how hard it is for the other person to say no.
Saying no is heavy. It costs something. You've found a way to make that cost free for yourself.
And so the cost goes somewhere else. It lands on everyone who asks.
Here's the weird part, the habit takes over.
Someone says, wanna ride home? Your mouth says, buzz.
Do you wanna sit with us? No, buzz, are you okay? No, you say, and it's the first time you actually mean it.
Zoe is seven. Every night for years, she knocks on your door with the same book.
And every night, you say the same thing. Sure, come in. For years, that was a free yes.
Now it's a $1,000 yes. You've been counting.
Last Thursday, she knocked. You said, not tonight, buzz.
She said, okay. And she took the book back to her room and you listen to her footsteps get smaller.
The next night, she didn't knock at all. You have $28 million.
You have never been so alone. A famous study from 1978 followed people who had won the lottery.
Not long after, they were no happier than people who hadn't.
Money is great at fixing problems. It is terrible at making you feel like somebody loves you.
And researchers who study loneliness have found that weak social ties are linked to something like a 26% higher risk
of dying early. That's not a feeling. That's a number.
You wonder if Warren Buffett is on to something.
He is often quoted saying that really successful people say no to almost everything, maybe so.
But he's also never had to say no to his little sister.
Then the offer comes. A man in a gray suit asks to meet you.
Chairman of a company with a name you've seen billboard in town, he pushes a tablet across the table.
On the screen is a number, $1 billion.
We call it the perfect refusal, he says. 24 hours, live stream.
Every single person who asks you for anything, you say no.
Say yes once and the deal is off. 40 million people have already signed up to watch.
$1 billion. For 24 hours of doing what you have been doing for months, you say yes.
Buzz, withdrawal, $1,000 gone.
Aldridge raises an eyebrow, that was a yes. I meant, I'll do it.
Say it again in a way that counts, you say I accept. The tablet goes green, the clock starts.
The stream begins at noon. By one you have a million viewers, by four, 10 million.
By nine there are 38 million people watching a 16 year old say no.
The chat scrolls so fast you can't read it. A woman asks if you wanna hold her baby.
No, a man asks for directions. A kid in a yellow fur kid from the very first day holds out a slice of pizza.
Free, no, the chat goes wild.
After every single no, the balance climbs.
Plus 1,000, plus 1,000. By hour 20, the number is $61 million and with the billion waiting at the end,
you could buy every roof in this town. At hour 20, your phone rings, it's Theo.
You haven't heard his voice in two weeks. You answer because the rules say you can pick up.
He had a heart attack at the shop. He's at St. Mary's and the doctor says he might not make it through the night.
He's awake though, he keeps asking for you. He says you're the only one who ever made him laugh at the hardware store.
Theo's voice cracks. Please, Pien, will you come?
It's 40 minutes away. I'll understand if you can't.
Behind you, Aldridge's producer is holding up four fingers. Four hours left.
Four hours until $1 billion. You look at the tablet, you look at the clock, you look at the camera and 38 million people look back.
You know exactly what happens if you say yes. The deal is dead, a billion dollars gone for one word.
The word you used to say without thinking a hundred times a day back when it was free.
Then you remember Mr. Reyes, the roof, the way he pretended he wasn't crying.
And you remember what mom said years ago, money comes and goes, people don't.
Theo, you say yes. Buzz, the screen goes red, deal terminated.
In the chat, 40 million people type it once. Nobody is sure what to say.
Aldridge stands up and for a second you think he'll shout. He just looks at the number on the tablet.
Then it you. You grab your jacket and run.
The stream follows you. Of course it does. A hundred cars on the road, a thousand drones overhead.
The camera crew in the van beside you films you sprinting through the hospital doors with your shoelaces untied.
40 minutes of road, you make it in 26.
In room 414, Mr. Reyes is propped up in bed with a thousand wires on his chest.
He sees you and smiles like you're late for a shift. There he is, the kid who lost a billion dollars.
He's seen it, everyone has. Sit, tell me a bad joke.
You sit, you tell him a very bad joke about a screwdriver.
He laughs so hard the monitor beeps faster and the nurse comes in to scold both of you.
Theo is standing in the corner holding his own face in his hands.
By morning, he's stable. By the end of the week, he's home.
And the news has a new name for you. Not the kid who says no.
They call you the boy who said yes. The headline reads, Teen walks away from a billion dollars to sit with a sick friend's dad.
The video of you running through the hospital doors gets 200 million views.
Aldridge doesn't pay the billion. He does announce a new wing at St. Mary's with Mr. Reyes' name on it.
You still have 60 million dollars. You have no idea what to do with it.
But on Sunday, mom calls. Dinner tonight? I know you're busy.
You look at the phone, you know the rule. A yes costs $1,000.
Yes, you say, buzz, you smile.
It is the best $1,000 you ever spent. That night, Zoe knocks on your door with her book's same book.
Same spot on the cover that she colored in with a purple marker.
Do you wanna read it? Yes, buzz. You read it three times.
Somewhere around the second time, she falls asleep against your arm and you don't move for an hour.
A week later, you're back on the sidewalk. The man in the yellow vest is there.
He sees you, hesitates and holds out a flyer. Free slice?
He asks in the voice of a man who has learned his lesson.
You take it. Yes, buzz, withdraw $1,000.
He stares at you. Seriously, you eat the slice right there on the curb.
It is a terrible slice. It's lukewarm, the cheese is sliding off and you have never tasted anything better.
Of course in the real world, nobody gets paid $1,000 to say no.
But the question is real. Saying no protects your time, your energy and your peace.
It's a skill and a good one. The trick is knowing which yeses are worth the price.
You walk home with the flyer in your pocket. Your phone buzzes one more time.
A notification you've never seen before. A text from an unknown number.
Nice work. Round two starts at midnight. Say anything but yes.
So here is the question. If you could earn $1,000 every time you said no, how many people would you refuse?
And if your best friend called with one yes between you and a billion dollars, would you have picked up the phone?
Tell us in the comments what you would do with $1,000 every time you said no.
And if you would have run to that hospital too, hit like and subscribe for more What Ifs.
